articles.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
articles.author: Michael Nalick, Assistant Professor of Management, University of Denver
paras: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.
This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.
But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions, it’s even more difficult.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks.

Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.
My research has found that risk to be high.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”

articles.title: The US-China AI race is real – but Trump’s recent moves on ‘super intelligence’ are unlikely to give America any advantage
articles.author: Ram Gopal, Professor of Information Systems Management, Warwick Business School, University of Warwick
paras: Donald Trump is insisting that people drop their use of the term artificial intelligence (AI), in favour of “super intelligence”. This started on September 29, when he signed an executive order telling federal agencies to call AI super intelligence, because, in the president’s view, “artificial” makes it sound fake.
On October 4, he followed up with a super intelligence force to coordinate the federal government’s effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the world in Super Intelligence”.

This AI force is led by Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Alongside him sit Federal Trade Commission chair Andrew Ferguson, the Pentagon’s technology chief Emil Michael and Scott Kupor, who runs the federal workforce.
The force reports to the president and his chief of staff and has 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities AI poses.

Is this serious national strategy or a branding exercise? The label itself tells us very little. What matters is whether the force can marshal what actually decides who leads in AI: compute, capital, talent and infrastructure. This is now a race, and the countries and organisations that move fastest and mobilise the most resources will hold a significant advantage.

Supporters can point to a genuine coordination problem. Responsibility for AI in Washington is scattered across intelligence, defence, competition policy, procurement and the civil service, which rarely act in concert.
Putting several of those agencies under one roof, reporting directly to the White House, could cut through that. Clayton has given a blunt assessment: “The risk of not being first is high.”

America also has a strong hand. According to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index, US private investment in AI reached US$285.9 billion (£217.24 billion) in 2025, roughly 23 times China’s US$12.4 billion (£9.42 billion). America’s largest tech firms are on track to spend more than US$650 billion on capital investment this year.

A body that helps clear bottlenecks the private sector cannot – grid connections, data centre permitting (approval), hiring technical talent into government – could add real value. Including the head of the federal workforce is a telling choice: governments have long struggled to recruit the people they need for AI.

Critics see something much thinner. The White House has not disclosed a budget, nor said whether the force will have regulatory powers or merely advise. It arrived shortly after leading firms, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and Nvidia, had signed a one-page White House accord committing to internal evaluations, external audits and board reviews.

Trump called it “morally binding”. But Democrat lawmaker Mark Warner, senior senator from Virginia, was scathing: “The president’s response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves,” he said.

To my mind, there are three deeper problems. First, the US does not control the trajectory of AI. The same Stanford report found that the performance gap between the best US and Chinese models has narrowed to 2.7%, down from double digits in 2023.

Beijing will pursue its own strategy whatever Washington calls its task force. Second, the actors that matter most are private. The frontier AI labs (those at the cutting edge) have enormous commercial and strategic incentives of their own – and the previously mentioned investment figures are overwhelmingly made up of private money.

The companies will cooperate where interests align, on energy or export controls, for example. But I would not expect them to commit fully to a government programme. A voluntary accord with no enforcement mechanism shows where the leverage lies.

The third problem is timing. The US midterm elections heavily shifted control of Congress in the Democrats’ favour. This could reshape both funding for AI and oversight. Building national AI capability is a multi-year effort, and what is created by executive action can be undone the same way. For instance, President Trump revoked Joe Biden’s AI executive order on his first day back in office.

There is also a tension in the mandate itself. The force is asked both to win a race and to protect the public, yet its leadership is drawn from the intelligence, defence and competition enforcement sectors rather than from AI safety. Those goals do not always point the same way, and the announcement about the super intelligence force says little about how they will be balanced.

Is this better than nothing? Absolutely. Coordination has value, and the force could become a serious mechanism for concentrating resources at a scale commensurate with the stakes. But the test is not the name. It is whether the body secures a substantial budget, gains real authority over approval for infrastructure, procurement and hiring, and survives the political cycle.

AI policy is at a turning point. Yet a name, like super intelligence, is just a slogan. Until we see what resources the super intelligence force can command, and whether it can execute quickly and sustain that effort, I would put relatively little faith in it changing the trajectory of AI.

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
articles.author: James A. R. Marshall, Director, Centre for Machine Intelligence, University of Sheffield
paras: OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.

Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning. As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it: “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”
OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science.

Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.
The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.

But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.

This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions. This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said: “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”

This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.

This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.

Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.
Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.
Protecting critical thinking

Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.

But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.
As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.

This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.

I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.

If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?
This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.

One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.

The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.

We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

articles.title: AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software
articles.author: Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University
paras: If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java.

For nearly three decades, the Java programming language has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet. While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of most large, behind-the-scenes server applications that power modern business, finance and government.

That ubiquity is why a new critical security alert from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide. Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, in a core Java component. If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code.

As a cybersecurity researcher who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered.
To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place.

Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on. Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the Java Virtual Machine. It is essentially a program that runs other programs. Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine.

In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data.

One of those routine tasks is Base64 encoding. Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols. Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64. When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it.
Inside the flaw and why AI matters

The newly discovered vulnerability resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine. This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk.

According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server.

If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile PHP vulnerability, another foundational web language. Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm Calif using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities.

Calif officials said the company alerted the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw.

Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts. Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years.
Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist. In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly.

First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it.
Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices. This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets.

Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward. Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet. Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – firewalls, load balancers and web proxies – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application.

Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, called tokens, directly to Java’s decoder. As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates.
As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices.

articles.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture – here’s how food scientists manufacture them
articles.author: Rohit Singh, Postdoctoral Researcher in Food Materials Science, West Virginia University
paras: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

Plant-based meat alternatives have become an increasingly prominent part of the food industry, driven partly by concerns about the sustainability of conventional meat production and the search for additional protein sources. One life-cycle assessment found that plant-based patties had a 77% lower climate impact than the Brazilian beef patties examined, although the results varied depending on the production systems and environmental measures considered.

But making a convincing meat alternative is not as simple as replacing animal protein with plant protein. How do you turn ingredients from peas, soybeans or wheat into something that looks, tastes and feels like meat?

When people think about protein, foods such as chicken, beef, eggs and milk often come to mind. However, plants are also important sources of protein. Soybeans, peas, wheat, lentils and other legumes contain proteins that can be extracted and used in food products.

Soy and pea proteins are widely used in plant-based meat alternatives. Wheat protein, or gluten, can also contribute to their structure and chewy texture. Researchers are also exploring other sources, including fava beans and mung beans, to expand the range of ingredients available.

But plant proteins behave differently. Some absorb more water, while others bind fat or form structures that hold ingredients together. These properties influence how a food feels when you bite into it. Choosing a protein therefore involves understanding how it behaves during processing, not just its nutritional value.
Why is making meat from plants so difficult?

Think about biting into a piece of roasted turkey breast. Its texture comes from the arrangement of muscle fibers, along with connective tissue, water and fat. Together, these components create firmness, juiciness and the chewing experience you associate with meat.

Plant proteins have structures that are different from animal muscle proteins. Mixing pea or soy protein with water does not automatically create meatlike fibers. Food scientists use processing methods that organize these proteins into structures that more closely resemble muscle.

Flavor matters, too. Fat adds juiciness and carries flavor compounds, while heating creates familiar roasted and savory aromas. A convincing meat alternative must bring together the right ingredients and processing conditions to reproduce these qualities.
Turning plant proteins into meatlike foods

One widely used method is extrusion. Protein-rich ingredients are mixed with water and pushed through a machine that applies heat and pressure while mixing the material. These forces unfold the proteins and help them interact.

As the mixture cools, the proteins form aligned, fibrous structures that resemble some features of meat. High-moisture extrusion uses more water during processing, which produces fibrous products with a more meatlike texture.

The final structure depends on factors such as the protein source, moisture content, temperature and processing conditions. These factors influence how proteins interact and form the fibrous structures found in plant-based meat alternatives.

Manufacturers can also add fats, starches, flavorings and other ingredients to improve the eating experience. Small changes in formulation or processing can make a considerable difference, affecting whether a product is firmer, softer, chewier or better at retaining moisture.
A potential future for meat alternatives
Another emerging approach is 3D food printing. Like a conventional 3D printer, a food printer builds an object layer by layer, depositing edible materials according to a digital design.

Our research explores protein-based food inks: mixtures designed to flow through a printer nozzle and hold their shape once deposited. Developing the right formulation is challenging because the material must be fluid enough to print but still firm enough to retain its shape. Researchers are applying similar principles to explore printing plant-based meat alternatives.

Instead of relying only on conventional manufacturing methods, 3D printing could allow researchers to control how different ingredients are arranged. For example, you could potentially deposit protein-rich materials and fat-containing ingredients in specific patterns to create different structures and textures.

Recent research on the 3D-printing of plant-protein-based meat analogs highlights how the formulation of the food ink and printing conditions influence how accurately a product can be printed and whether it holds its shape. However, a printed product that looks like meat must still deliver the expected texture, flavor and eating experience.

Plant-based meat alternatives are not necessarily intended to replace traditional meat. They offer consumers additional choices, but making them appealing, affordable and consistent remains a challenge. Scientists continue to study how proteins, ingredients and processing work together to create the textures and flavors people enjoy.

The next time you see a plant-based burger or turkey alternative, remember that making it involves much more than replacing animal protein with plant protein. Technologies such as extrusion and 3D food printing are helping scientists explore new ways to turn plant ingredients into meatlike foods.
Rohit Singh is affiliated with West Virginia University.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached 1 light-day from Earth, the first human-made object in space to reach that distance
articles.author: Matthew Shindell, Curator of Planetary Science and Exploration, Smithsonian Institution
paras: In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space.

During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then traveled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium: the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating.

But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. On Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16 a.m. EST, Voyager 1 will become the first human-built object of any kind to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. At that point, it will have traveled about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers), more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto. Afterward, it will take light, including communication signals, 24 hours to travel between the spacecraft and Earth.
This achievement is remarkable on many levels. This spacecraft, a functioning relic of 1970s technology, has survived well past its expected lifespan.

Of course, the spacecraft no longer works as well as it did in its prime. Eight of its original 10 instruments are not operating, and the output from its plutonium-238 power source degrades a little bit each year. Every so often, a lost signal or technical failure puts Voyager 1 in the headlines again. And, within the next decade, scientists may receive the last signal ever from this far-flung object.

But, at least for now, both Voyagers continue to send back data that is helping scientists characterize the unknown territory beyond the solar system. As a space history curator responsible for the National Air and Space Museum’s planetary science collection, I’ve studied how space exploration has changed dramatically over the past 50 years.

Through it all, the Voyager probes have consistently collected valuable scientific data that has shaped researchers’ understanding of the solar system – and even what lies beyond it. They’ve also helped set public expectations for what a successful mission looks like.
Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, 16 days after the identical Voyager 2, from NASA’s launch complex in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Voyager 2 launched first, but Voyager 1 quickly overtook it.

These spacecraft were big both in size and in ambition. Each is about the size of a small car, with an extended magnetometer boom, carrying instruments that measure magnetic fields, more than 50 feet (15 meters) long.

Each probe explored the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and returned images from these planets that had higher resolutions than anything returned by their predecessors, Pioneer 10 and 11. They imaged the turbulent atmosphere of Jupiter, discovered faint rings around the planet and captured new details of the rings of Saturn and its many moons.

Voyager 2 would go on to explore Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, completing a grand tour of the solar system, that omitted Pluto. Voyager 1 launched after Voyager 2 so it could be set on a course that took it to Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.

On Nov. 12, 1980, Voyager 1 flew within 4,034 miles (6,492 km) of Titan and returned images of the moon that showed a world shrouded in a dense and substantial atmosphere. Now, several decades later, NASA’s Dragonfly mission is slated to take flight in the mid-2030s and investigate Titan’s atmosphere.

This trajectory allowed the probe to image several of Saturn’s other moons and even discover a few new ones. But it also sent Voyager 1 on a course that flung it away from the plane of the planets’ orbits.

It has been traveling in that direction ever since, crossing several milestones along the way. It crossed the orbit of Pluto in 1989. On Feb. 14, 1990, before powering off its cameras for the last time, it captured a series of 64 images that together became the first “family portrait” of the solar system.

There is no clear definition of what it means to leave the solar system. But Voyager 1 has felt less and less of the Sun’s influence as it moves into interstellar space. In December 2004, it crossed the “termination shock”: the outer boundary of the influence of the high-energy particles that make up the solar wind.

On Aug. 15, 2012, it left the protection of the Sun’s magnetic field, making it more susceptible to cosmic radiation. As it crossed this boundary, its instruments detected a sparse layer of superheated plasma: charged gas atoms that are so energetic that their electrons are ripped away from their nuclei. Scientists nicknamed this boundary the “Wall of Fire.”
The spacecraft continues to travel through interstellar space, recording how the space environment changes as you move farther away from the Sun with data from two of its original instruments.

Meanwhile, failing memory, computer glitches, power issues and challenges with an aging propulsion system have led to several nail-biting moments over the past decade in which it seemed scientists might lose contact with the mission forever.
Remarkably, NASA engineers have always found a way to use backup thrusters and reroute data to keep the spacecraft operating, long enough to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
So what actually is one light-day?

When talking about the distance from the Earth to the Moon, or from the Earth to Mars or Venus, you’d still use miles or kilometers. But once you travel farther than the distance between Earth and its nearest neighbors, the number of miles starts to increase exponentially.

Outside of the inner solar system, scientists start to use a larger unit of measure: the astronomical unit (AU), one of which equals the distance between the Sun and Earth. The Kuiper Belt, for example, where Pluto is found, covers a wide swath between 30 and 50 AUs from the Sun.

The inner solar system, with Earth and all of the rocky planets, is only an incredibly small fraction of the solar system, and the units of measurement used on Earth don’t really scale well as you move farther away from the planet.

Outside of the solar system, scientists start to talk in terms of time: light-years, or, more precisely, the distance light travels in a year. One light-year is equivalent to 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion km), or 63,241.1 AU. The nearest neighboring star to our solar system is Proxima Centauri, which is about 4.25 light-years away.
Voyager 1 is now, after 50 years, almost 1 light-day away from Earth. That’s a big distance compared with our usual frame of reference, but it’s still just a fraction of a light-year.

While traveling at 37,844.49 mph (60,773 kmh), it will take another 300 years for Voyager 1 to encounter the Oort Cloud that surrounds the solar system, which no one has actually seen, and another 30,000 years to pass through it.

From a galactic perspective, after nearly 50 years, Voyager 1 is out the door but has barely entered the front yard. Covering multiple light years and actually making it near a neighbor’s house, like Alpha Centauri, which refers to a system of stars that orbit with Proxima Centauri, would be a 75,000-year trip, if Voyager 1 were headed that way.

Until scientists develop technologies to carry people between the stars, like those found in science fiction – if they ever do – people will continue to send increasingly capable robotic spacecraft as our emissaries to help us learn more about the space and worlds beyond our reach.

Maybe, many thousands of years from now, some other space-faring civilization from a distant planetary system will discover Voyager 1. The spacecraft famously carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record that includes greetings, messages, sounds and music, along with encoded images of life on Earth.

Many people continue to believe that the exploration of the cosmos can represent the peaceful aspirations of all of humanity. And they continue to want to connect with this great exploratory endeavor by signing their names, literally and culturally, on these great works of technology.
We may never hear back from anyone. But we will at least have tried to fill the insurmountable distances of deep space with a bit of ourselves and our culture.

articles.title: Nasa’s Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, reaches distance milestone of one light-day from Earth
articles.author: Ed Macaulay, Lecturer in Physics and Data Science, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, has marked an extraordinary milestone. At 10:16:07 GMT (05:16:07 EST) on November 18, 2026, it reached a distance of one light day from Earth.

One light day is the distance that light can travel in a vacuum in 24 hours and is equal to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometres). A light year, often used to measure distances from Earth to astronomical objects like other stars, is the distance light can travel in space in one year.

For some perspective, the Artemis II mission set a new record for the greatest distance from Earth travelled by humans, at 252,756 miles, in April 2026. It takes light just over 1.3 seconds to travel this distance. Voyager 1 is now more than 63,000 times further away than the human distance record set by Artemis II.

Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to take advantage of a planetary alignment that occurs about once every 175 years. This enabled spacecraft to explore the planets of the outer solar system by using gravitational assists to travel from one planet to the next.
The significance of this rare planetary alignment was recognised in the mid 1960s by Gary Flandro, who at the time was a graduate student at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory near Los Angeles.

Thomas Paine, who served as Nasa administrator from March 1969 until September 1970, reportedly sold the mission to President Richard Nixon with some historical context: “The last time the planets were lined up like that, President Jefferson was sitting at your desk. And he blew it.”

Voyager 1 had an “identical twin” spacecraft – Voyager 2 – that actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1. Voyager 1 carried out flybys of Jupiter and Saturn, while Voyager 2 visited Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

The Voyager missions returned a treasure trove of images that has transformed our knowledge of the solar system. This effort was overseen by the Voyager Imaging Team, consisting of nine scientists chosen by Nasa in 1972.

The team was led by Brad Smith, from the University of Arizona, and included Carl Sagan at Cornell University, who would become widely known for his work to popularise science on television and in other media.
Of the scientists selected for the imaging team, eight were from the US and one was British: astrophysicist Garry Hunt from University College London.
When I spoke to Professor Hunt recently, he explained that being the only team member from the UK was “an opportunity to open up planetary science in this country”.

The unique planetary alignment meant there was only a brief window to launch both Voyager spacecraft. Professor Hunt described this period as particularly intense, noting that there was “no time for tea breaks”.

After 18 months of spaceflight, Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979. Professor Hunt noted: “that’s when the fun started”. Voyager 1 studied the complex dynamics of the huge storm in Jupiter’s atmosphere known as the Great Red Spot. The spacecraft also detected aurorae and lightning, as well as discovering active volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io.

After gathering data on the Jovian system, Voyager 1 continued on, reaching Saturn in November 1980. The spacecraft revealed previously unseen structures in the planet’s majestic rings, including wedge-shaped features in Saturn’s B ring which scientists dubbed “spokes”.
It also resolved craters on the Saturnian moons Enceladus and Mimas, and a thick nitrogen atmosphere on the large moon Titan.

Recalling this period, Garry Hunt told me: “We honestly didn’t know what those funny marks were in the rings, the spokes”. He added that the largest crater on Mimas made it look “like the Death Star from Star Wars”.

Perhaps the most famous image from the mission was taken nine years later, in early 1990. Carl Sagan had been lobbying for nearly a decade for Voyager 1 to take one last photograph of our home planet before its cameras were permanently powered down. Professor Hunt explained that “we wanted to take the family portrait”.

The photograph, which became known as the Pale Blue Dot, revealed planet Earth, as Sagan described, as “a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam”. Hunt described the image to me as “perhaps one of the most important pictures ever taken”.

After 35 years of spaceflight, Voyager 1 crossed the boundary of the heliosphere. This is a region of electrically charged particles – plasma – that surrounds the Sun and the planets. When it passed this threshold, Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft made by humans to enter interstellar space.

My colleague Dr Chris Chen, reader in space plasma physics, at Queen Mary University of London, describes the heliosphere as a “bubble of plasma”. He explained that Voyager 1 made some surprising discoveries when it traversed this boundary.

Rather than finding the expected change in magnetic field direction, Voyager 1 detected a magnetic field that remained broadly aligned with the field inside the heliosphere. Instead, the spacecraft found a dramatic reduction in the number of solar cosmic rays, which suggests that the dynamics of space plasma marks the true boundary of interstellar space.

After nearly half a century of spaceflight, Voyager 1 is still operational, and still providing valuable scientific data. As well as extraordinary observations and discoveries about the largest planets in our solar system, Voyager 1’s Pale Blue Dot photograph has become one of the classic images of space exploration.

At the height of the mission, Professor Hunt recalled working eighteen-hour days: “We were pathfinders, it was tough”. Reflecting on the Voyager programme, he recalled that “everything we touched, everything we did, was historic”. Nearly half a century after its launch, Voyager 1 continues its journey into interstellar space.

It is now so distant from Earth that signals travelling at the speed of light take a full day to reach it, and another day for a response to return. This extraordinary milestone provides an opportunity to appreciate the unique perspective that Voyager 1 has given us on our own place in the solar system.

articles.title: Your gut bacteria helps your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
articles.author: Zheng Kuang, Associate Professor of Biological Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the scientific journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

Gut microbes convert dietary signals into molecules that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times. In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce.
When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system fueled obesity.

Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience rhythmic shifts of day and night. Your eyes and brain use light signals to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability. Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is associated with a range of health disorders.

However, light is not the only timekeeper. Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome. They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity.

Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the daily biological rhythms of hosts. My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms in the small intestine and alters them in the colon. These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity.
But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time.

We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize phytate – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients. Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption.
Through this pathway, microbes align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat, which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption.
Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions.
People have co-evolved with their gut microbiota for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits.

For most of human history, food was scarce. We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions. To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation. We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule grew taller and healthier than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited.

However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories. Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge. We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway promotes excess fat uptake in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity.
Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for. This is an example of evolutionary mismatch.

articles.title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI
articles.author: Deven Desai, Professor of Business Law and Ethics; Associate Director for Law, Policy, and Ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting.

In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that it’s ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide. The state of Kentucky later filed suit, claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation.
Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused.
Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda.
I am a former litigator and a professor of business law, and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm.

But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability. Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants.
Abnormally dangerous software

Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store. Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble.

Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity, such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it.

AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “the utmost care to prevent the harm.”

An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox – a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network – but loses control of it. The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose.

One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage. Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous. But damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent.

Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes.

Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting. In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable. Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category.

Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. “Design defects” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use.

AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way. In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers,” according to a Brookings Institution report.

I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues.

The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.
Deven Desai owns shares in Google, Inc. He received unrestricted research gifts from Google, Inc. and Facebook, Inc. a decade ago. He has not been employed by Google since 2010.

articles.title: What AI regulation could learn from the most hazardous industries in the world
articles.author: Palie Smart, Professor in Operations Management and Head of School Management, University of Bristol
paras: Darren Jones MP, the former chief secretary to the prime minister under Keir Starmer, recently called for a new multinational treaty governing the safe development and use of superintelligence (where AI substantially surpasses humans across most cognitive tasks).
He also argued that Britain’s growing reputation for AI safety and trustworthiness made it a good conduit for such collaboration.

What I found most interesting about this intervention was not the question of whether AI could pose a threat to humanity. Instead, it was a management and organisational question sitting underneath it: “can our systems of governance keep pace with the development of AI intelligence while also ensuring it is safe?”

We are at a moment in history where global tech leaders and some of their employees believe there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. But humans are still struggling to understand the potential consequences of AI; by the time we do it may be too late to act.

However, we must be careful to distinguish this prediction from the current risks and what might happen as AI systems become able to independently improve themselves (full recursive self-improvement) and move towards superintelligence.

I concur with calls for a multinational treaty and for the UK to take a leading role. As a business scholar, I also believe research from some business schools can inform us about managing and organising systems whose complexity, speed and autonomy are increasing faster than our capacity to understand them.

This is familiar territory in high hazard industries such as nuclear energy and aviation. Here, two theories are particularly relevant: normal accident theory, associated with the US sociologist Charles Perrow, and high reliability theory, associated with the work of American political scientist Todd LaPorte. Taken together, they could provide a powerful framework for thinking about AI safety and regulation.

Normal accident theory begins with an uncomfortable proposition. In complex, interdependent systems, such as nuclear power plants or spacecraft built to carry humans, accidents are not necessarily the consequence of individual incompetence, negligence or bad design. They can emerge from the interaction of multiple components in ways that are difficult to anticipate.

In such systems, events happen rapidly. When something unexpected takes place, there may be little time to intervene between one potential failure and the next. This can lead to a cascading error, with the potential to cause a catastrophe. An often-used example is the partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, US, in 1978. The accident occurred because of a combination of mechanical malfunction, instrument faults and human factors.

The risks further increase when you add AI agents into such a complex system – AI agents are systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions. Examples might include financial systems, software development systems, scientific databases in labs or even systems that connect lots of agents.

In any such system, an individual component – including the AI agent – might meet acceptable quality thresholds; the difficulty lies in the interactions between them and our understanding of these interactions. Part of the problem is that we know agents’ behaviour can be unpredictable: recent reports have described AI agents behaving in ways that their developers did not expect.

The UK government has highlighted risks associated with increasingly capable AI agents and has stressed the importance of testing frontier AI models and developing a scientific understanding of their capabilities.
If AI systems become more autonomous, more interconnected and faster moving, the conventional idea of a “human in the loop”, to correct major errors, could become increasingly challenging.

High reliability theory offers a counterpoint. The high reliability tradition emerged from research into organisations that were operating technologies where failure could have catastrophic consequences, such as nuclear power plants, aircraft carriers and air traffic control.

Its central insight is almost the opposite of a pessimistic reading of normal accident theory. Essentially, it says that organisations can develop practices and cultures that allow them to operate extraordinarily complex technologies with very low failure rates. In fact, we have seen this with the electricity system, space travel and bioengineering.

These organisations achieve high reliability because their baseline assumption is that they are not safe. They remain attentive to hints of bigger problems, do not automatically dismiss anomalies, learn from near misses and failures and build redundancy – for example, backing up offline systems and providing kill switches.

They routinely rehearse failure, establish operational processes, adhere to regulation for safety and assurance, comply with professional standards and certification schemes and have independent oversight. High reliability organisations give experts the authority to challenge decisions. They continuously learn from their performance.

This provides a very different way of thinking about AI governance. Instead of asking simply, “how do we regulate AI?” we should ask: “what would a high-reliability organisation look like if AI was embedded throughout it?”
This suggests that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off technical test before deployment. It must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.

This is where the current political conversation about AI regulation risks being too narrow. Governments need to understand what frontier laboratories are developing. But government cannot realistically sit permanently inside every AI company and inspect every model.

Nor can legislation anticipate every technical configuration that AI will take. The UK government recognises it must cultivate trustworthiness in AI through assurance. Assurance asks whether there is credible evidence that a system is behaving within defined boundaries, whether those boundaries are appropriate, whether risks are being monitored and whether someone is accountable when they are breached.
The aircraft industry has engineering standards, certification regimes, professional qualifications, independent inspection, incident reporting and regulatory oversight.
Nuclear power operates within an elaborate ecosystem of safety engineering and regulatory assurance. Financial institutions and medicine both have sophisticated systems of assurance.

AI is becoming increasingly consequential, yet its assurance infrastructure remains comparatively immature. This is particularly striking given the speed at which frontier systems are developing. The institutional challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation, but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful.

A potential new multinational treaty on the safe and regulated development of superintelligence would frame AI safety as a rapidly evolving global challenge. At the same time, it potentially creates a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the UK to help shape the emerging architecture of AI governance.

articles.title: Catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden – and a drag on productivity
articles.author: Karen Feigh, Professor of Cognitive Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: By now, almost everyone has asked an AI agent a question, only to realize that the answer seems not quite right. Something might be missing or wrong or out of date. An executive assistant told me she uses AI tools for drafting itineraries and briefings, but she’s caught enough issues that she now builds time into her workflow to thoroughly check for inaccuracies and biases.

Therein lies the catch: AI responses can improve productivity, but the gains are often countered by time and mental energy spent determining whether the output is accurate and appropriate. This is the verification burden.

At a deeper level, the burden is the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work that is partly delegated to a system, while retaining responsibility for the final product. Cognitive engineer David Woods described this problem back in 1985 as the responsibility-authority double bind: Automation exercises practical authority, yet responsibility remains with the human.

I am a cognitive engineer, and I study how people work with automated decision-support systems. Generative AI verification is the latest instance of a long-standing human-factors problem: a new kind of necessary work brought about by use of a new technology.

AI workers are exchanging some skills related to creating and transforming information for separate skills that resemble supervising an extraordinarily fast and polished intern. The difficulty is that this intern delivers both good and bad work in the same confident voice, provides few clues about where scrutiny is needed, and bears no responsibility for the consequences.
Verifying instead of creating

Research shows that verifying new information is a different task than creating it, and it’s not a simpler one. A meta-analyis of 86 studies revealed that people remember what they produced far better than anything they only read. The same is true for understanding information. Research also shows that material that is easy to read and understand seems more credible, and people therefore consider it more likely to be true.

But humans do not always vet AI responses. Instead, they tend to weigh their own internal costs and benefits to decide when to check. Overreliance on AI output is hard to stop, too. One research team found that adding simple explanations of the AI’s reasoning did not eliminate the quandary people felt in committing the time and energy needed to check. People tend to generalize agents as either capable or incapable and nothing in between.

Economics scholars have found real productivity improvements from using generative AI in office work. But a randomized trial of experienced software developers found no gains, and completion times increased when a verification step was included. Surprisingly, the developers believed they had been faster when using AI, yet their completion time increased by 19%.
And a large study of consulting teams found that using AI outside of a person’s area of expertise resulted in more people reaching the wrong conclusion.
These studies do not establish that there is a universal verification “tax,” but they show why the speed alone of generating output is an incomplete measure of productivity.
Verification can feel burdensome in terms of cognitive load, time spent and motivation.

People feel a cognitive burden because verification is fundamentally different from creation. You generally know when something you are creating is “done,” or is at least sufficient for the task. When to stop verification is less obvious. A worker must decide what to check and how; they do not know whether an error exists, where it might be or what form it might take.

This is similar to airport security screening, where an unusual threat gets missed more often than a common one because it is easy for inspectors to conclude that rare threats are not present. This burden is greater when AI helps someone generate work that exceeds their ability to evaluate it. A recent study found that AI reasoning helped people catch mistakes on easy questions but not hard ones, when help was needed most.

A time burden arises because instead of ending work, finding an error starts another cycle of correction and then rechecking. Research into how people evaluate AI-generated suggestions has found that the more work needed to fix an identified mistake, the less likely people are to actually fix it.

Finally, verification carries a motivational burden. Creation produces visible progress, but verification may find only that nothing was wrong. When automation usually performs well, checking can feel unproductive, and people may gradually become less vigilant. This pattern was found two decades ago in a study of people working with automated decision-making systems.

Together, these burdens result in a skill swap. In a recent survey, knowledge workers said their critical thinking was moving from production toward verification. Workers also need to learn how to recognize the capabilities and limits of a specific AI agent, including omissions and biases.

These skills are different, but they are not necessarily easier, and they might not even be in the skill set of workers who excel at creation. Companies and organizations therefore cannot treat verification as a natural step that carries no effort. If workers remain accountable for AI-assisted output, I believe that they must also be given the time, training and authority needed to verify it.

The measurement of productivity gains cannot include just how quickly AI produces a first draft. Instead, the measure is whether the entire human-AI workflow produces trustworthy work at a lower total cost.

articles.title: Why does your body store fat in your butt?
articles.author: Cara Ocobock, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, University of Notre Dame
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why does your body store fat in your butt? - Ellen, age 8, Cambridge, Massachusetts
Have you ever wondered why some parts of your body are firm, like your elbows, while other areas, like your butt, are squishier?
The difference is due to what scientists call fat distribution, and researchers are still trying to understand why bodies store fat in some places but not in others.
All animals have fat in their bodies, even insects. Bears even put on up to 400 pounds (180 kilograms) of additional body fat, the equivalent of 544 large cheese pizzas, to survive hibernation.
Fat is an important and constantly changing part of all bodies, including those of humans and our evolutionary ancestors.
Fat, also called adipose tissue, is one kind of connective tissue that helps hold your body together.

For a long time, scientists thought that adipose tissue was mainly a storage place for the extra energy your body doesn’t use from the food you eat. While fat is a great source of stored energy, it also has many other functions. There are even different kinds of fat.

Visceral fat serves as a sort of protective bubble wrap, surrounding and filling in the spaces between your internal organs. Subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat between your skin and your muscle that you can pinch, is a protective cushion and helps to keep you warm by insulating you like a coat.
Fat also produces and responds to hormones, a type of chemical messenger, to regulate how your body uses energy and to tell you when you are hungry or full.
Different kinds of fat also have different jobs. White fat is the kind of fat most people are familiar with and performs the functions mentioned above.
You may be less familiar with brown fat, which is brown because it contains a lot of mitochondria: the parts of your cells that produce the energy your body needs to perform all its functions.

Not all animals have brown fat, but humans do. Scientists know that brown fat performs a special function to heat your body when you get cold. It doesn’t store energy, like white fat does, to help your body move.

When you were a baby, you had a lot of brown fat along your torso to help keep you warm because your body wasn’t mature enough to maintain your body temperature. As you grow older, you have less brown fat. It is only located just above your collar bone and along your major deep blood vessels, like your aorta.
Why do humans store fat where we do?

Researchers don’t know enough yet about brown fat to know why it is in just a few parts of the body. It is possible that it’s near the neck and around major blood vessels to help insulate the blood and keep overall body temperature in a healthy warm range.
As for white fat, there appear to be three main factors that determine where your fat gets stored: genetics, hormones and age.
Certain genes direct fat to accumulate in the butt, while other genes tell it to collect on the torso.

Hormones like estrogen, which affects almost every system in all bodies but is typically higher in females, direct more subcutaneous fat to gather in the butt, thighs and backs of the arms. Cortisol, the stress hormone, seems to direct visceral fat to accumulate in the belly area.

But why isn’t fat evenly distributed throughout the body? Well, having a lot of fat around your elbows and knees would limit your ability to bend your arms and legs. Storing a lot of fat around your head would possibly put your brain at risk of overheating. Other parts of your body, like hips, butts, breasts and thighs, don’t have these risks – maybe that’s why we store fat there.
Why do people have fat at all?

Don’t be fooled: A lot of animals that look fat, like a hippopotamus, actually aren’t. Hippos only have around 2% body fat, the percentage of how much of your body mass comes from fat; while the average human woman has over 30% body fat.

In the rest of the animal kingdom, biologists typically only see a lot of body fat among hibernating or marine mammals. For the hibernators, the fat serves as energy storage for long, cold winters. For marine mammals like seals and whales, that extra fat is like a giant puffy coat helping to keep them warm in the cold depths of the ocean.
Humans do not hibernate, nor do we live in the ocean, so why do we have a lot more fat than all other primates and most mammals?

Anthropologists like me, who study how the human body has evolved over time, think it has to do with the lifestyle of our evolutionary ancestors who had to gather and hunt to survive. Gathering and hunting were not always reliable food sources. We think our ancestors developed the ability to put on extra fat as a food insurance policy. When food was difficult to find, they could rely on their extra fat stores to carry them through until food became available again.
Researchers are still trying to determine when this extra fat storage evolved. We have one line of evidence from small stone figures known as Gravettian statues.
These ancient statues from 25,000 to 28,000 years ago depict feminine figures who carry a lot of extra body fat. Archaeologists have found them all throughout Europe and Russia.

The way the ancient artists depicted fat on these figures matches how fat looks on bodies today. This accuracy has led researchers to believe that the makers of the Gravettian statues knew how individuals with greater body fat actually looked, meaning at least some people at this time did put on a lot of extra fat.

Europe and Russia back then were much colder than they are today, supporting the idea that our ancestors would have needed the extra fat to get through the extremely cold winters when food was harder to find.
So, the next time you poke at your butt fat, remember that fat is a really important part of our bodies, performs lots of different functions, and is likely evolutionarily ancient for us humans.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.
